title: Explain closures in JavaScript
prompt: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give an example of when you would use one.
idealAnswer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scope even after the outer function has finished executing. The inner function keeps a reference to its outer scope, so the variables stay alive as long as the closure exists. Closures are commonly used for data privacy, factory functions, and memoization.
keyPoints: function retains access after the outer function returns
used for data privacy, factory functions, or memoization
hints: Think about what happens to variables when an outer function returns.

title: Explain the event loop
prompt: What is the event loop in JavaScript and how does it handle asynchronous code?
idealAnswer: The event loop is what lets JavaScript, which is single-threaded, handle asynchronous operations without blocking. The call stack runs synchronous code; async operations like timers and network calls are handed to the Web APIs / runtime. When they finish, their callbacks go into task queues (microtasks vs macrotasks). The event loop continuously checks: when the call stack is empty, it pushes pending callbacks from the queue back onto the stack. Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (timers, I/O).
keyPoints: Web APIs / runtime handle async work
